whenToUse.text: Use an accordion to condense long content into scannable headers that users open on demand.
Use an accordion for FAQ-style content, where users pick the questions they need.
Users reveal one or more panels on demand, so content stays hidden until they open it.

whenNotToUse.text: Do not use an accordion for primary navigation.
Do not put content users must read in full or need to compare in an accordion, because collapsed panels hide it.
Avoid nesting accordions; if you must, indent and limit to one level.

variants.text: Use Bordered when you want full dividers separating the items.
Use Borderless when items should be separated only by spacing, with no outline, and keep the spacing between items consistent.

content.text: Write each title as a start-aligned label that names its section.

D1.text: Documentation / Usage: An accordion is a vertical stack of collapsible sections that condenses long content into scannable headers.

D12.text: Documentation / Usage: Items separated by full dividers.

D13.text: Documentation / Usage: Items separated only by spacing; no outline.

D14.text: Documentation / Usage: Single- vs multiple-expand is behavior (expandMode), not a Figma variant. Bordered and Borderless are the Style variant.

D15.text: Documentation / Usage: • To condense long content into scannable headers that users open on demand.

D16.text: Documentation / Usage: • For FAQ-style content, where users pick the questions they need.

D19.text: Documentation / Usage: • For content users must read in full.

D21.text: Documentation / Usage: • ② Title — start-aligned label for the section.

D24.text: Documentation / Usage: The title is start-aligned and the icon end-aligned on the same row. The trigger spans the full header width.

D25.text: Documentation / Usage: Items stack vertically at full width — never side by side. Spacing between items is consistent; borderless accordions rely on it as their only separator. Avoid nesting accordions; if you must, indent and limit to one level.

D8.text: Documentation / Usage: An accordion condenses long content into scannable headers. Users reveal one or more panels on demand — which also means content stays hidden until they open it.

R2.text: Accordion guidance: Do not hide content people need to compare or always read in an accordion.

questions: When should you choose Bordered over Borderless? The docs describe how each looks, but not when to use it.
What should people use instead of an accordion for primary navigation? The evidence names no other component in this system.
Is there guidance on title length or wording, for example phrasing FAQ titles as questions?

whenToUse.text: Use an alert to show a short, sentiment-coded message inline on the page.
Use an alert to give feedback inline, for example the result of an action or a change in status.
Add an action when the person can respond to the message, and a close button when they can dismiss it.

whenNotToUse.text: Do not use an alert for an urgent message that must interrupt the page: use a Dialog, because alerts stay inline.
Do not use an alert for information that belongs in the page content, and do not show several alerts for one event.
Do not put a large primary button in an alert: use a Ghost, Sm Button for the action.

content.text: Keep the message short.
Give every alert a headline.
Add supporting text below the headline only when the message needs a description.

D1.text: Documentation / Usage: An alert shows a short, sentiment-coded message inline on the page, with an optional action and close button.

D13.text: Documentation / Usage: • ③ Headline — required title.

D14.text: Documentation / Usage: • ④ Supporting text — optional description.

D20.text: Documentation / Usage: Use a Ghost, Sm Button for the action — matching the alert's compact footprint.

D21.text: Documentation / Usage: Don't use a large primary button — it overpowers the alert.

D22.text: Documentation / Usage: • Required on every alert.

D24.text: Documentation / Usage: • Optional description below the headline.

D28.text: Documentation / Usage: • Close — dismisses the alert, collapsing it out of the layout.

D29.text: Documentation / Usage: • Action — runs the alert's action; while it's running, the action button shows its loading state.

D34.text: Documentation / Usage: • Dialog — for urgent messages that must interrupt the page; alerts stay inline.

D8.text: Documentation / Usage: Alerts surface feedback inline on the page. Each sentiment has its own colors and icon. The action and close buttons are real Button instances, and the icon is a real Icon instance.

R1.text: Notification guidance: Use a notification to tell people about the result of an action or a change in status.

R2.text: Notification guidance: Do not use a notification for information that belongs in the page content.

R3.text: Notification guidance: Do not show several notifications for one event.

The sources say what each Sentiment looks like (colors and icon) but not when to use it. When should designers pick Neutral rather than Info, and what situations call for Warning versus Danger?
Should alerts that use role="alert" (assertive) map to particular sentiments, such as Danger and Warning?
When should an alert be dismissible (With Close), and when should it stay on the page?
Is there guidance on writing the action label, such as length or wording?
Size has Sm and Md: when should each be used?

whenToUse.text: Use AutoplayToggle as the pause and play control in a carousel that advances on a timer.
Add it whenever a carousel autoplays: always pair autoplay with a visible, reachable pause control.
It gives users a way to stop autoplay at any time.

whenNotToUse.text: Do not add AutoplayToggle to a carousel that advances only manually: use NavControl and PaginationDot for advancing.
Do not use AutoplayToggle as a general on/off setting outside a carousel: use Switch.
Do not use AutoplayToggle as the only way to move between slides: give users controls, pagination or swipe as well.

content.text: AutoplayToggle is icon-only, so give it an accessible name.

D10.text: Documentation / Usage: Manual advance, finite — the edge control disables at the first and last slide.

D11.text: Documentation / Usage: Advances on a timer, always paired with a visible pause control.

D18.text: Documentation / Usage: • ② Navigation controls — Prev and Next NavControl buttons.

D20.text: Documentation / Usage: • ④ Pagination — PaginationDots showing position and count; the active dot is larger.

D24.text: Documentation / Usage: Always pair autoplay with a visible, reachable pause control.

D25.text: Documentation / Usage: Don't autoplay without a pause control.

D26.text: Documentation / Usage: Don't hide navigation with no alternative way to advance.

D27.text: Documentation / Usage: Give users a way to advance — controls, pagination or swipe.

D37.text: Documentation / Usage: • Autoplay — Playing or Paused (AutoplayToggle).

D8.text: Documentation / Usage: A carousel shows a subset of items at once when they exceed the available space. In this system it's assembled from three components — NavControl, PaginationDot and AutoplayToggle — around your own viewport and slides.

D82.text: Documentation / Accessibility: • An AutoplayToggle with Playing and Paused states, so autoplay can always be stopped.

R1.text: Switch guidance: Use a switch for a setting that takes effect as soon as it is turned on or off.

S1.text: Other switch components in this design system: Switch.

questions: Should AutoplayToggle switch to Paused automatically when autoplay pauses on hover, focus or a hidden tab, or only when the user presses it?
Once autoplay stops after the user interacts with a control, can the user restart it with AutoplayToggle, or does it stay Paused?
What accessible names should the Playing and Paused states use (for example, "Pause slides" and "Play slides")?

whenToUse.text: Use AvatarGlyph to represent a person or entity at a glance with an image, an icon or initials.
Use it on its own when you need the avatar alone, without a name or email beside it.
Use it to represent a person with their photo or initials, or a system account, bot or non-person entity with an icon.
Use AvatarGlyph where it is static and decorative: it has no hover or interactive states, so it does not look clickable.

whenNotToUse.text: Do not use AvatarGlyph alone to identify someone next to their name and email: use AvatarIdentity.
Do not use AvatarGlyph when the avatar opens a profile card or menu: use AvatarIdentity, which has hover, focus and other interactive states.
Do not rely on the avatar as the only way to identify a person: show their name too.

variants.text: Use Text for initials, the first letter of the first and last name, when you have no photo of the person.
Use Icon for system or bot accounts, placeholders and entities that aren't people.
Use Image for a photo of the person.

content.text: Build initials from the first letter of the first and last name (Jane Doe → JD), and shrink the font to fit rather than clip.
Derive an initials avatar's color from a hash of the user's name or ID so the same person always gets the same color; don't assign a random color on each render.
Give image avatars alt text that names the person, not "avatar" or "user photo", and if the image fails to load, fall back to the icon (if configured), then to initials.

whenToUse.text: Use AvatarIdentity to identify someone next to their name and email.
It pairs an AvatarGlyph with a name, an optional email and an optional trailing icon, such as a chevron for a menu.
Use it for people and for entities that aren't people, such as system or bot accounts.
Use its interactive states when the avatar opens a profile card or menu.

whenNotToUse.text: When you only need the avatar (image, icon or initials) with no name, use AvatarGlyph instead.
Don't use an avatar as the only way to identify a person: show their name too, which is what AvatarIdentity is for.
When the avatar is purely decorative and opens nothing, don't make it look clickable: a decorative avatar has no hover styling.

content.text: Set the name and email with the Name and Email text properties; the email is a secondary line.

whenToUse.text: Use a badge to show a status, a count, a label or a notification on another element.
Use Status to show an item's state: success, warning, error, info or neutral.
Use a Numeric badge to show a count, such as unread notifications, and a Dot badge to show that something needs attention without a count.
Use a Text badge to tag an item with a short label, and make it dismissible when users should be able to remove it.

whenNotToUse.text: Don't use a badge as a primary action, a button or a main navigation target: use a Button.
Don't use a badge for anything longer than a short label, a single count or one icon: no paragraphs, multiple icons or nested badges.
Don't reuse a status color for an unrelated meaning.

variants.text: Use Filled as the default style; the docs preview the default badge with Style=Filled.
Use Outlined for a badge drawn with a border instead of a fill, as its name says.
Use Subtle for a lower-emphasis fill, as its name says.

content.text: Keep a text label short, and make the label carry the meaning so it doesn't rely on color alone.
Cap large counts at {max-count}+ (for example 99+) instead of showing the full number.
Place a badge next to or on the element it describes, and don't let its content overflow or stretch the parent layout.

D1.text: Documentation / Usage: A badge is a small element that communicates a status, a count, a label or a notification on another element.

D10.text: Documentation / Usage: Each status color maps to exactly one meaning and is never reused for another.

D11.text: Documentation / Usage: • To show the status of an item — success, warning, error, info or neutral.

D12.text: Documentation / Usage: • To show a count, such as unread notifications — Numeric.

D13.text: Documentation / Usage: • To show that something needs attention without a count — Dot.

D14.text: Documentation / Usage: • To tag an item with a short label — Text; a dismissible badge lets users remove it.

D16.text: Documentation / Usage: • As a primary action, button or main navigation target — use a Button.

D17.text: Documentation / Usage: • For more than a short label, a single count or one icon — no paragraphs, multiple icons or nested badges.

D29.text: Documentation / Usage: Place a badge next to or on the element it describes. Content must never overflow, break or expand the parent layout.

D3.text: Documentation / Usage: Preview of the default variant (Status=Success, Style=Filled, Type=Text, Size=Sm) in the light and dark modes of semantic.color. Static preview — no interactive source (Storybook or prototype) is linked yet.

D32.text: Documentation / Usage: Cap large counts: show {max-count}+ (e.g. 99+).

D33.text: Documentation / Usage: Don't render a wider raw count.

D34.text: Documentation / Usage: Use a status color only for its meaning.

D35.text: Documentation / Usage: Don't reuse a status color for an unrelated meaning.

D36.text: Documentation / Usage: • A short label or a single count — nothing longer.

D37.text: Documentation / Usage: • If the count is above max-count (default 99), show {max-count}+.

D46.text: Documentation / Usage: • Button — use for actions; a badge must never act as a primary action.

D72.text: Documentation / Style: Dot badges use the same fill (Filled, Subtle) or border (Outlined) tokens.

D8.text: Documentation / Usage: A badge annotates another element with a status, a count or a short label. It never stands alone as a primary control.

D91.text: Documentation / Accessibility: • Text badges carry their meaning in the label, not in color alone.

P4.text: Status: Success, Warning, Error, Info, Neutral

R2.text: Badge guidance: Do not use a badge for actions: use a button or link.

R3.text: Badge guidance: Do not use colour alone to carry the meaning; use the text too.

What is the guidance for choosing Size (Sm, Md, Lg)?
What should a clickable badge's one action be? D42 and D43 mention clickable badges, but no source says when to make one.

whenToUse.text: Use a breadcrumb to show where the current page sits in a content hierarchy.
Use it to give one-click navigation back to each parent level.
Treat breadcrumbs as secondary navigation that sits alongside your main navigation.

whenNotToUse.text: Do not use a breadcrumb as the primary navigation of the app.
Do not use breadcrumb items to start actions: use a button.

variants.text: Use Link for each ancestor level in the trail, which the user can click to go to that level.
Use Current for the final item only, the page the user is on, shown as plain text that is not interactive.
Use Collapse when the trail has more items than maxItems, so the middle levels hide behind an ellipsis while the root and current page stay visible.

content.text: Give each item except the last the name of the parent level it links to, and give the final item the name of the current page.
Let long labels truncate with an ellipsis, and keep the full label available in a tooltip.
Use one separator style, chevron or slash, for the whole trail.

D33.text: Documentation / Usage: • Long labels truncate with an ellipsis; the full label stays available in a tooltip.

D34.text: Documentation / Usage: • The final item names the page the user is on.

D38.text: Documentation / Usage: • Current — Default only; never interactive.

D42.text: Documentation / Usage: Clicking a link goes to that level. Clicking the collapse trigger reveals the hidden items. The current page and separators do nothing.

whenToUse.text: Use a button to trigger an immediate action in the current context, such as submitting a form, confirming a choice, opening something or deleting an item.
Use the button's emphasis levels to keep the most important action on a screen the easiest one to find.
Use one primary action in a context and pair it with lower-emphasis actions.
Keep every button in a group the same size.

whenNotToUse.text: Do not use a button when activating it takes the user to another page or location: use a text link instead.
Do not place two primary buttons in the same context, because they read as equally important.
Do not use a button only to show or hide content inline: use a disclosure or accordion.

variants.text: Use Primary to mark the single most important action in a context.
Use Secondary for supporting actions of lower weight next to a primary one.
Use Ghost for supporting actions of lower weight next to a primary one.
Use Danger only for destructive or irreversible actions such as delete or remove; for anything else use Primary, Secondary or Ghost.

content.text: Write the label as a verb that describes the action, such as Save, Delete or Open.

whenToUse.text: Use a checkbox for a square control that people select or clear, on its own, as a labeled field, or as a titled group of fields.
Use it to turn one option on or off, or to let people choose any number of options from a list.
Pick the layer you need: CheckboxControl for the bare box, CheckboxField for the control with its label and messages, or CheckboxGroup for a titled group of fields.
Use CheckboxControl as the leading or trailing control of a list item in multi-select lists.

whenNotToUse.text: Do not use a checkbox when people may choose only one of several options: use radio buttons.
Do not use a checkbox for a setting that applies at once: use a switch.
Do not place CheckboxControl alone where the option needs a visible label: use CheckboxField, which adds the label and value text.

variants.text: Use Unselected when the option is not chosen.
Use Selected when the option is chosen; the box shows a check.
Use Indeterminate for a mixed selection; the box shows a dash and is exposed as aria-checked="mixed".
Use Error-Unselected for an unchosen option in a field in the Invalid state, which adds an error border and message.
Use Error-Selected for a chosen option in a field in the Invalid state.
Use Error-Indeterminate for a mixed selection in a field in the Invalid state.

content.text: Write the Value text to describe what checking the box means.
Use the Label text for the field or group title.
Add a description under the label or helper text under the field only when the option needs supporting text.
